summary: When a town sells something holy, it may use the money only to buy something holier, never something less holy. Rabbi Yehudah says a town may not sell its holy things to one person.

chunks.he: בְּנֵי הָעִיר שֶׁמָּכְרוּ רְחוֹבָהּ שֶׁל עִיר,
chunks.en: People of a town who sold the town square,
chunks.explain: The square was a bit holy because people davened there sometimes.
chunks.st: Residents of a town who sold the town square,
chunks.stMore: which was at times used for public prayer and therefore attained a certain degree of sanctity, may use the proceeds of the sale only to purchase something of a greater degree of sanctity.

chunks.en: may buy a shul with the money.
chunks.st: They may therefore purchase a synagogue with the proceeds of the sale.

chunks.en: If they sold a shul,
chunks.st: If they sold a synagogue,

chunks.en: they may buy an aron.
chunks.explain: The aron is the cabinet that holds the sefarim.
chunks.st: they may purchase an ark in which to house sacred scrolls.

words.note: The holy ark for the sefarim.

chunks.en: If they sold an aron, they may buy cloths.
chunks.st: If they sold an ark, they may purchase wrapping cloths for the sacred scrolls.

chunks.en: If they sold cloths, they may buy sefarim.
chunks.st: If they sold wrapping cloths, they may purchase scrolls of the Prophets and the Writings.

chunks.en: If they sold sefarim, they may buy a Sefer Torah.
chunks.st: If they sold scrolls of the Prophets and Writings, they may purchase a Torah scroll.

chunks.en: But if they sold a Sefer Torah,
chunks.st: However, the proceeds of a sale of a sacred item may not be used to purchase an item of a lesser degree of sanctity. Therefore, if they sold a Torah scroll,

chunks.en: they may not buy sefarim.
chunks.st: they may not use the proceeds to purchase scrolls of the Prophets and the Writings.

chunks.en: If they sold sefarim, they may not buy cloths.
chunks.st: If they sold scrolls of the Prophets and Writings, they may not purchase wrapping cloths.

chunks.en: If they sold cloths, they may not buy an aron.
chunks.st: If they sold wrapping cloths, they may not purchase an ark.

chunks.en: If they sold an aron, they may not buy a shul.
chunks.st: If they sold an ark, they may not purchase a synagogue.

chunks.en: If they sold a shul,
chunks.st: If they sold a synagogue,

chunks.en: they may not buy the town square.
chunks.st: they may not purchase a town square.

chunks.en: And the same is true for the money left over.
chunks.explain: Extra money must also be used only for something holier.
chunks.st: And similarly, the same limitation applies to any surplus funds
chunks.stMore: from the sale of sacred items, i.e., if after selling an item and purchasing something of a greater degree of sanctity there remain additional, unused funds, the leftover funds are subject to the same principle and may be used to purchase only something of a degree of sanctity greater than that of the original item.

chunks.he: אֵין מוֹכְרִין אֶת שֶׁל רַבִּים לְיָחִיד,
chunks.en: We may not sell a holy thing of the many people to one person,
chunks.st: They may not sell a sacred object belonging to the community to an individual,
chunks.stMore: even if the object will still be used for the same purpose,

chunks.en: because that lowers its holiness.
chunks.st: due to the fact that by doing so they downgrade its degree of sanctity,
chunks.stMore: as an item used by fewer people is considered to have a lower degree of sanctity than one used by many;

chunks.en: These are the words of Rabbi Yehudah.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: The Rabbis said to him:

chunks.en: If so,
chunks.st: If so,

chunks.he: אַף לֹא מֵעִיר גְּדוֹלָה לְעִיר קְטַנָּה:
chunks.en: it would also not be allowed from a big town to a small town!
chunks.explain: But that is surely allowed, so selling to one person is allowed too.
chunks.st: by your logic, it should also not be permitted to sell a sacred object from a large town to a small town. However, such a sale is certainly permitted, and therefore it must also be permitted to sell such an object to an individual.

summary: Rabbi Meir says a shul may be sold only if the sellers can take it back. The Sages say it may be sold forever, but not to be used for four disrespectful things.

chunks.en: We may not sell a shul
chunks.st: They may sell a synagogue

chunks.he: אֶלָּא עַל תְּנַאי שֶׁאִם יִרְצוּ יַחֲזִירוּהוּ,
chunks.en: except on the condition that if they want, they can get it back.
chunks.st: only with a stipulation that if the sellers so desire it, the buyers will return it to them;

chunks.en: These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:

chunks.en: We may sell it forever,
chunks.st: They may sell a synagogue with a permanent sale for any usage,

chunks.en: except for four things:
chunks.st: except the following four things, which would be an affront to the synagogue’s previous sanctity:

chunks.en: for a bathhouse, a tannery, a mikveh, or a washroom.
chunks.explain: A tannery is where animal skins are made into leather; it smells bad.
chunks.st: For a bathhouse, where people stand undressed; or for a tannery [burseki], due to the foul smell; for immersion, i.e., to be used as a ritual bath, where people also stand undressed; or for a lavatory.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: We may sell it to be a courtyard,
chunks.st: They may sell a synagogue for the generic purpose of serving as a courtyard,

chunks.en: and the buyer may do with it whatever he wants.
chunks.st: and then the buyer may then do with it as he wishes, even if that is one of the above four purposes.

summary: Even a shul that was destroyed is still holy, so we may not use it for everyday things. But if grass grows there, we leave it, so that people will be sad and want to rebuild it.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Yehudah also said,
chunks.st: And Rabbi Yehuda said further:

chunks.en: A shul that was destroyed,
chunks.st: A synagogue that fell into ruin
chunks.stMore: still may not be used for a mundane purpose.

chunks.en: we may not say a eulogy in it,
chunks.st: Therefore, one may not eulogize in it.

chunks.en: and we may not stretch out ropes in it,
chunks.st: And nor may one stretch out and repair ropes in it.
chunks.stMore: The wide expanse of the synagogue would have been particularly suitable for this.

chunks.en: and we may not spread out traps in it,
chunks.st: And nor may one spread animal traps within it.

chunks.en: and we may not spread out fruit on its roof,
chunks.st: And nor may one spread out produce upon its roof to dry.

chunks.en: and we may not make it into a shortcut,
chunks.st: And nor may one make it into a shortcut.
chunks.stMore: The halakha that a synagogue in disrepair still may not be used for mundane purposes is derived from a verse,

words.note: A path to walk through to save time.

chunks.en: as it says,
chunks.st: as it is stated:

chunks.en: "And I will make your holy places empty."
chunks.st: “And I will bring desolation to your sanctuaries” (Leviticus 26:31).
chunks.stMore: The fact that the word “sanctuaries” appears after the word “desolation” indicates that

chunks.en: They are still holy even when they are empty.
chunks.st: their sanctity remains upon them even when they are desolate.

chunks.en: If grass grew up in it,
chunks.st: However, if grass sprang up of its own accord in the ruined synagogue,

chunks.en: he should not pull it out,
chunks.st: although it is not befitting its sanctity, one should not pick it,

chunks.en: because it makes people sad.
chunks.explain: Seeing it will remind them to rebuild the shul.
chunks.st: due to the anguish that it will bring to those who see it. It will remind them of the disrepair of the synagogue and the need to rebuild it.

summary: In the weeks around Adar, special parshiyos are read: Shekalim, Zachor, Parah and HaChodesh. On special days, we stop the regular order and read about that day.
stIntro: On four Shabbatot during and surround-ing the month of Adar, a Torah portion of seasonal significance is read.

chunks.he: רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר שֶׁחָל לִהְיוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת,
chunks.en: When Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbos,
chunks.st: When the New Moon of Adar occurs on Shabbat,

chunks.en: we read Parshas Shekalim.
chunks.explain: It tells about the half-shekel everyone gave.
chunks.st: the congregation reads the portion of Shekalim on that Shabbat.

chunks.en: If it falls during the week,
chunks.st: If the New Moon occurs during the middle of the week,

chunks.en: we read it the Shabbos before, and skip the next Shabbos.
chunks.st: they advance the reading of that portion to the previous Shabbat, and, in such a case, they interrupt the reading of the four portions on the following Shabbat,
chunks.stMore: which would be the first Shabbat of the month of Adar, and no additional portion is read on it.

chunks.en: On the second Shabbos, Zachor.
chunks.explain: Zachor tells us to remember what Amalek did.
chunks.st: On the second Shabbat, the Shabbat prior to Purim, they read the portion: “Remember what Amalek did” (Deuteronomy 25:17–19),
chunks.stMore: which details the mitzva to remember and destroy the nation of Amalek.

chunks.en: On the third, Parah Adumah.
chunks.explain: Parah Adumah tells how to become tahor from the tumah of a dead person.
chunks.st: On the third Shabbat, they read the portion of the Red Heifer [Para] (Numbers 19:1–22),
chunks.stMore: which details the purification process for one who became ritually impure through contact with a corpse.

chunks.en: On the fourth, "This month is for you."
chunks.explain: It tells about the month of Nissan and the korban Pesach.
chunks.st: On the fourth Shabbat, they read the portion: “This month [haḥodesh] shall be for you” (Exodus 12:1–20),
chunks.stMore: which describes the offering of the Paschal lamb.

chunks.en: On the fifth, we go back to the regular order.
chunks.st: On the fifth Shabbat, they resume the regular weekly order of readings and no special portion is read.

chunks.en: For all special days we stop the order:
chunks.st: For all special days, the congregation interrupts
chunks.stMore: the regular weekly order of readings, and a special portion relating to the character of the day is read.

chunks.en: on Rosh Chodesh,
chunks.st: This applies on the New Moons,

chunks.en: on Chanukah and on Purim,
chunks.st: on Hanukkah, and on Purim,

chunks.en: on fast days, on the maamados, and on Yom Kippur.
chunks.explain: The maamados were groups of people who davened while their Kohanim served.
chunks.st: on fast days, and on the non-priestly watches, and on Yom Kippur.

summary: This mishnah tells which part of the Torah we read on Pesach, Shavuos, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos.

chunks.en: On Pesach we read the parshah of the Yamim Tovim
chunks.st: On the first day of Passover, the congregation reads from the portion of the Festivals

chunks.en: in Toras Kohanim.
chunks.st: of Leviticus (Leviticus 22:26–23:44).

chunks.en: On Shavuos, "Seven weeks."
chunks.st: On Shavuot they read the portion of “Seven weeks” (Deuteronomy 16:9–12).

chunks.en: On Rosh Hashanah,
chunks.st: On Rosh HaShana they read the portion of

chunks.en: "In the seventh month, on the first of the month."
chunks.st: “And on the seventh month on the first of the month” (Leviticus 23:23–25).

chunks.en: On Yom Kippur,
chunks.st: On Yom Kippur they read the portion of

chunks.en: "After the death."
chunks.explain: It tells about the avodah of the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur.
chunks.st: “After the death” (Leviticus 16).

chunks.he: בְּיוֹם טוֹב הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁל חָג קוֹרִין
chunks.en: On the first day of Sukkos we read
chunks.st: On the first Festival day of Sukkot they read

chunks.en: the parshah of the Yamim Tovim in Toras Kohanim,
chunks.st: from the portion of the Festivals of Leviticus (Leviticus 22:26–23:44),

words.en: that is in the Torah of

chunks.en: and on all the other days of Sukkos,
chunks.st: and on the other days of Sukkot

chunks.en: we read about the korbanos of Sukkos.
chunks.st: they read selections from the portion of the offerings of Sukkot (Numbers 29:12–39).

summary: This mishnah tells what we read from the Torah on Chanukah, Purim, Rosh Chodesh and fast days. It also teaches that we read about each Yom Tov on its own day.

chunks.en: On Chanukah, the parshah of the Nesi'im.
chunks.explain: The Nesi'im were the heads of the shevatim who brought gifts for the Mishkan.
chunks.st: On each day of Hanukkah they read selections from the portion of the dedication of the altar by the tribal princes (Numbers 7).

chunks.en: On Purim, "And Amalek came."
chunks.st: On Purim they read the portion of “And Amalek came” (Exodus 17:8–16).

chunks.en: On Rosh Chodesh,
chunks.st: On the New Moon they read the portion of

chunks.en: "And on your Roshei Chodesh."
chunks.st: “And in the beginnings of your months” (Numbers 28:11–15).

chunks.en: At the maamados, the story of how the world was made.
chunks.st: And in the non-priestly watches they read the act of Creation (Genesis 1:1–2:3).
chunks.stMore: The Jewish people were divided into twenty-four watches. Each week, it would be the turn of a different watch to send representatives to Jerusalem to be present in the Temple to witness the sacrificial service. Those remaining behind would fast during the week, from Monday to Thursday, offer special prayers, and read the account of Creation from the Torah.

chunks.en: On fast days, the brachos and the curses.
chunks.st: On fast days, they read the portion of blessings and curses (Leviticus, chapter 26).

chunks.en: We do not stop in the middle of the curses,
chunks.st: One should not interrupt the reading of the curses by having two different people read them.

chunks.en: but one person reads all of them.
chunks.st: Rather, one person reads all of them.

chunks.en: On Monday, Thursday, and Shabbos at Minchah,
chunks.st: On Mondays, and on Thursdays, and on Shabbat during the afternoon service,

chunks.en: we read in the regular order,
chunks.st: they read in accordance with the regular weekly order,
chunks.stMore: i.e., they proceed to read the first section of the Torah portion that follows the portion that was read on the previous Shabbat morning.

chunks.en: but they do not count toward the order.
chunks.explain: On Shabbos morning, we start again from the same place.
chunks.st: However, these readings are not counted as a progression in the reckoning
chunks.stMore: of reading the Torah portions, i.e., they do not proceed on Monday to read the section that immediately follows the section read on Shabbat during the afternoon, and then the following section on Thursday. Rather, until the reading on the following Shabbat morning, they return to and read the same first section of the Torah portion that follows the portion that was read on the previous Shabbat morning. On Festivals and holidays, they read a portion relating to the character of the day,

chunks.en: as it says,
chunks.st: as it is stated:

chunks.en: "And Moshe told the special times of Hashem
chunks.st: “And Moses declared

chunks.en: to the Bnei Yisrael."
chunks.st: to the children of Israel the appointed seasons of the Lord” (Leviticus 23:44),

chunks.en: Their mitzvah is that we read
chunks.st: the mitzva of the Festivals is that the people should read the portion relating to them,

chunks.en: each one at its own time.
chunks.st: each one in its appointed time.
